references.text: Job asks what hope the godless have when God demands his soul back: 'For what hope has a godless man when God cuts him off, when He takes away his life?' (Job 27:8). The same theme that God demands the soul back from one who has lived without God.

The psalmist acknowledges the transience of life and the uncertainty of who will inherit one's wealth: 'He gathers it but does not know who will get it' (Psalm 39:7). A direct parallel to Jesus' question, 'what you have gathered, whose will it be?'
The psalm describes how the rich man dies and must leave his wealth to others (Psalm 49:11). The theme that riches cannot save from death is central in the parable.
'Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring' (Proverbs 27:1). The rich man planned for many years ahead but did not know he would die that night.

Ecclesiastes complains that he must leave all his toil to another who has not worked for it (Ecclesiastes 2:18-19). The same frustration underlies Jesus' parable: everything the rich man gathered, others will receive.
Ecclesiastes describes a man whom God gives wealth but does not allow to enjoy it (Ecclesiastes 6:1-2). A parallel to the rich fool who never got to enjoy what he had accumulated.

Isaiah condemns those who eat, drink, and are merry without regard for the Lord, with the attitude 'let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die' (Isaiah 22:13). The rich man's attitude in the parable reflects exactly this self-satisfied outlook on life.
Isaiah pronounces woe upon those who add house to house and field to field (Isaiah 5:8). A parallel to the greed of the rich man and his ever-growing storehouses.
'Riches do not profit in the day of wrath' (Proverbs 11:4). The accumulated goods of the rich man could not save him on that night when God demanded his soul.

James warns against planning for the future without taking God into account: 'Tomorrow we will go to such and such a city… and make money' – 'You do not know what tomorrow will bring' (James 4:13-14). A direct parallel to the overconfident plans of the rich man.
Paul reminds us that 'we brought nothing into the world, and we can take nothing out of it' (1 Timothy 6:7). This underscores the futility of the rich man's hoarding.

Jesus encourages his disciples to sell what they have and give to the poor, thus storing up treasure in heaven that does not decay (Luke 12:33). A contrast to the rich fool who only gathered for himself.
